title: Elodie and the Inventory
premise: Wren Iversen, a night librarian in a city that never quite sleeps, has spent twelve years orbiting his dying mother without ever saying what she means to him. When Mireille Okonkwo-Bass, the last fluent speaker of a vanishing language called Lissune, asks him to become her final student, he discovers that her tongue has no word for goodbye — only phrases for 'until the memory returns.' As Mireille's own mind begins to fail and Wren's mother's dementia deepens in parallel, he must transcribe a dying language while learning, at last, to speak plainly to the woman who raised him. The novel ends with Wren recording the final Lissune lesson — a song about leaving — and then driving through dawn to his mother's bedside, where he says everything out loud, properly, before her memory goes entirely.
about_author: Casper Sterling is the pen name of a former night-shift archivist who spent six years cataloguing oral histories from endangered-language projects. They write quietly devastating literary fiction about people who love each other too late and almost say so.

chapters.title: The Hours That Stay Open
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. We meet the night library, its insomniac regulars, and Wren's ritual of drafting letters to his mother he never sends, tucked into returned books. Emotional beat: tender avoidance; the reader sees a man fluent in everything except feeling.

chapters.title: A Woman Who Counts Her Words
chapters.summary: Mireille arrives at closing time asking for help finding 'a student, the last one.' Wren deflects her to the reference desk; she leaves a card written in an alphabet he can't read. POV: Wren. Beat: curiosity cracking through routine.

chapters.title: Visiting Hours
chapters.summary: Wren visits his mother, Odile, at Fernwood Care Home; she calls him by his dead father's name and he lets her, as always. His sister Thea confronts him about his silence. POV: Wren. Beat: guilt sharpened into a wound.

chapters.title: The Grammar of Staying
chapters.summary: Mireille returns; Wren agrees to one lesson, telling himself it's professional interest. She teaches him greetings and explains Lissune has no future tense — only 'the not-yet-remembered.' POV: Wren. Beat: reluctant wonder.

chapters.title: What Thea Keeps
chapters.summary: Thea's POV. She finds the unsent letters hidden in their childhood home and reads them alone at night, furious and heartbroken on their mother's behalf. Beat: the cost of Wren's silence seen from outside.

chapters.title: Lessons in the Not-Yet-Remembered
chapters.summary: Lessons become routine. Mireille shares how she lost her students to emigration and death, and why she chose Wren — she saw him shelving books 'like someone putting things back where they belong instead of forward.' POV: Wren. Beat: found family taking root.

chapters.title: Slippage
chapters.summary: Mireille forgets a word mid-sentence for the first time; later that week, Odile mistakes Wren for a stranger and he flees early. The two declines mirror each other. POV: Wren. Beat: dread; time becoming an antagonist.

chapters.title: The Recording Project
chapters.summary: Wren proposes recording every lesson; Mireille resists — a language on tape, she says, is a photograph of a person. He convinces her it's for him, not history. POV: Wren. Beat: negotiation between preservation and living.

chapters.title: Letters Found
chapters.summary: Odile finds one of Wren's old unsent letters in a box of books and asks Thea about it; Thea lies to protect him, then demands he finally visit honestly. POV: Thea. Beat: loyalty straining against truth.

chapters.title: The Song About Leaving
chapters.summary: Mireille begins teaching the Lissune farewell cycle — five songs sung when someone departs, none meaning goodbye forever. Wren realizes she is teaching him how to lose her. POV: Wren. Beat: foreboding wrapped in beauty.

chapters.title: Almost
chapters.summary: At Fernwood, Odile has a lucid hour and asks Wren directly why he never says what he feels; he almost answers, then the moment closes like water. POV: Wren. Beat: the title emotion — the near-miss that defines him.

chapters.title: Mireille's Daughter
chapters.summary: Simone, Mireille's estranged daughter, arrives intending to move her mother to assisted care far away, viewing Wren as a stranger exploiting an old woman. POV: Simone. Beat: threat to the found family; competing loyalties.

chapters.title: Two Kinds of Forgetting
chapters.summary: Simone sits in on a lesson and hears her mother sing a lullaby she hasn't heard since childhood; her certainty wavers but she holds firm on the move. POV: Simone. Beat: grief disguised as practicality.

chapters.title: The Archive Argument
chapters.summary: Wren and Simone clash over what Mireille owes — to memory, to family, to herself. Mireille interrupts them both with a story about her own mother's silence. POV: alternating. Beat: the theme made explicit: loyalty vs. truth.

chapters.title: Winter Lesson
chapters.summary: Mireille's lapses lengthen; she teaches the fourth farewell song and mistakes Wren for a student from 1974, then recovers and weeps. He stays all night. POV: Wren. Beat: devotion deepening into fear.

chapters.title: The Unsent Stack
chapters.summary: Thea gives Wren the box of letters she found; reading twelve years of his own almosts, he understands the shape of his cowardice. POV: Wren. Beat: reckoning; the lowest point before change.

chapters.title: Moving Day
chapters.summary: Simone arrives with movers; Mireille refuses, speaking a full unbroken paragraph of Lissune — her longest in years — asserting her right to finish teaching. Simone relents to a trial month. POV: Simone. Beat: climax of the Mireille thread; dignity winning.

chapters.title: The Fifth Song
chapters.summary: Mireille teaches the final farewell song, then tells Wren plainly: this was never about the language; it was about showing him how to leave someone well. POV: Wren. Beat: revelation; the mentor's true gift named.

chapters.title: Night Call
chapters.summary: Odile suffers a serious decline; at the hospital, Wren finally speaks — clumsily, completely — telling her everything in the letters aloud while she still knows his face. POV: Wren. Beat: the emotional climax; saying it out loud.

chapters.title: Until the Memory Returns
chapters.summary: In the quiet after, Wren and Thea sit with Odile together, no longer performing around the illness. Mireille visits and sings softly at the bedside in Lissune. POV: Thea. Beat: reconciliation; siblings reunited in honesty.

chapters.title: The Last Fluent Speaker
chapters.summary: Mireille dies in early spring, mid-dictation, her last recorded word unfinished. Wren completes the archive and donates it to the library's open shelves, where insomniacs will find it. POV: Wren. Beat: elegy; grief transmuted into offering.

chapters.title: Open Hours
chapters.summary: Epilogue. Wren keeps the night desk, teaches a small Lissune study circle of strangers, and writes his mother a letter he actually sends. Final line echoes the first unsent letter, now finished. POV: Wren. Beat: resolution; the art of almost becomes the practice of saying.
